headline: Rhode Island federal court voids DOJ grant conditions in survivor-services case
dek: A final ruling led by the Rhode Island Coalition Against Domestic Violence removes federal conditions that providers said threatened funding for shelters, crisis response and legal assistance nationwide.
body: A federal judge in Rhode Island has set aside U.S. Department of Justice grant conditions that domestic-violence and sexual-assault service providers said could restrict who they serve and how they operate. The Sept. 29 summary-judgment ruling in Providence gives a Rhode Island-led coalition of 25 state organizations a final judgment in a case that reached well beyond the state.

The order by U.S. District Judge Melissa R. DuBose says the department did not adequately explain its decision to attach the conditions to grants administered through the Office on Violence Against Women and the Office of Justice Programs. Rhode Island Current reported that the court found no sufficient, contemporaneous explanation showing that officials had meaningfully considered the conditions’ effects on providers and survivors. The [public court record](https://ecf.rid.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/show_public_doc?2025cv0279-78=) is the controlling document.

The challenged requirements touched on politically contested issues including diversity, equity and inclusion programs, gender identity and service to immigrants. The Rhode Island Coalition Against Domestic Violence and its partners argued that the federal government was using grant eligibility to impose new policy requirements without the reasoning required by the Administrative Procedure Act. The [ACLU of Rhode Island’s case update](https://www.riaclu.org/news/rhode-island-court-rules-in-favor-of-domestic-violence-and-sexual-assault-survivors-protecting-crucial-grants-to-support-victims-of-violence-nationwide/) says later conditions also could have prevented providers from serving some noncitizen survivors or people unable to immediately prove citizenship.

That distinction matters because these grants support practical services rather than only administrative projects. Rhode Island Current described the federally funded work as including legal help, housing assistance and crisis counseling. The programs are rooted in the Violence Against Women Act, the 1994 federal law that established a continuing national role in supporting services for people affected by domestic and sexual violence. The DOJ’s [fiscal-year 2026 award guidance](https://www.justice.gov/ovw/award-condition-general-appropriations-law-restrictions-use-federal-award-funds-fy2026) separately shows how broadly the department applies conditions to grants made under its funding notices.

The case began in 2025 after the coalition challenged the grant terms. A federal court first blocked an earlier set of restrictions, according to the ACLU, and the department later added conditions involving immigration status and other subjects. In April 2026, the court issued preliminary relief while the claims proceeded. The September ruling now resolves the merits of the challenge by vacating the conditions rather than leaving providers to operate under a temporary pause.

Rhode Island’s regional role is unusually broad. The plaintiff coalition includes the Massachusetts Coalition Against Sexual Assault and Domestic Violence, the Maine Coalition to End Domestic Violence and the Vermont Network Against Domestic and Sexual Violence, along with organizations from other states. The [Rhode Island Current report](https://rhodeislandcurrent.com/2026/09/29/ri-federal-judge-strikes-down-trump-grant-restrictions-for-domestic-violence-groups/) lists 25 plaintiff organizations representing 22 states and the District of Columbia.

The court’s remedy is also broader than a ruling limited to one Rhode Island provider. The order explains that setting aside the challenged conditions as a whole is necessary because a provider-by-provider remedy would be impractical. That means the decision addresses the grant terms themselves, while leaving the underlying federal programs and ordinary grant requirements in place. It does not decide every dispute over federal funding or guarantee that individual providers will receive a particular award.

The immediate effect is to remove the disputed certifications and restrictions that the plaintiffs said could force a choice between accepting federal money and altering survivor services. The public sources reviewed for this report did not identify a government appeal or a new replacement policy after the judgment. Providers and advocates will still have to follow the remaining statutory and grant-administration rules, but the contested conditions can no longer serve as the basis for withholding these awards under this case’s ruling.
